No, it isn't. You aren't supposed to "set out to disprove" anything. You set out to answer something, which is very different. No one who sets foot in a laboratory determined to prove their pet idea right or their rival's idea wrong at all costs has any business laying hands on the equipment. Their bias will infect the data.
Why does challenging a conclusion equate to "determining to prove their pet idea right or their rival's idea wrong at all costs"?

You don't challenge the conclusion before you even do the work. You do the work, with absolutely no preconception of how the results are going to land, and then, after you have collected the data, you perform an objective assessment, which leads to either confirming or challenging the conclusion of the other scientist. It is a loaded word to speak of "challenging" or "disproving" a publication before you have even begun the research.
They call it peer review. If it's not peer reviewed, it's not valid. If your claim is accurate it can be reproduced, and that's actually exactly how science works.

You're talking about the intent. But science itself, which is going with the scientific method and experimentation, is removed from intent. Science is a method of observation. So even if you do an experiment specifically so you can disprove someone, it's still science.

You can end up disproving someone, but you shouldn't call it that until after the data is in. The proper method when attempting to recreate someone else's work is to approach it with no preconception of how it's going to turn out, and certainly with no aim of showing it will be wrong. A good scientist will take care to keep his or her language neutral until after the research has been performed.
